intro: To create a Chrome profile on Mac, open Google Chrome, click the Profile icon at the top right, and choose Add Chrome profile. Then sign in with a Google Account or stay signed out, and pick a name, photo, and color scheme.
tldr: Click the Profile icon at the top right of the Chrome window, then choose Add Chrome profile.
Sign in with a Google Account to save the profile's data there, or stay signed out to skip sign-in.
Pick a name, a photo, and a color scheme so you can spot the profile at a glance.
Some Mac guides list Profiles > Add Profile in the menu bar. Google's help page does not, so check your screen.

blocks.text: What a Chrome profile does on your Mac

A Chrome profile is a separate browser setup inside the same Chrome app. Each profile keeps its own sign-in, sync settings, name, photo, and color scheme. Many people use one profile for work and another for personal browsing. A shared family Mac can hold a profile for each person, so everyone sees their own bookmarks and sign-in.

Profiles also keep your Google accounts apart. Google's help page says that signing in saves bookmarks, passwords, and other settings to your Google Account. You can then reach them on other devices where you are signed in. That is useful. It also means you should pick the account for each profile on purpose.

A Chrome profile is not the same as a Mac user account. Your Mac account controls the whole computer, including its files, login, and system settings. A Chrome profile only controls the browser. If you want separate desktop files, a separate macOS user account is the right tool.

Profiles are also different from Incognito and Guest. Incognito is a private window that runs inside your current profile. Guest browsing lets someone use Chrome without signing in to your profile. Google's shortcut table lists ⇧⌘N for a new Incognito window. It lists ⇧⌘M for the profile, guest, and password menu.
Create a profile from the Profile icon

This is the route Google's help page describes. The page covers computers in general, so it does not name Mac menus. The steps below use the labels from that page. Match them to what you see on your screen. You can start from any open Chrome window.
Create a profile from the menu bar or the ⋮ button

Some Mac guides describe two other routes. ShiftPlus says you can go to Profiles > Add Profile in the menu bar. It also says you can click the ⋮ button, choose the current profile name, and then click Add New Profile. Google's help page does not show either label. Treat them as backups, and check what your screen shows before you click.

blocks.text: Use whichever route matches your screen. All of them lead to the same setup: a name, a photo, and a color scheme. The Profile icon route is the one Google documents, so start there. Fall back to the other routes only when the first one does not work.
Sign in or stay signed out

Sign in when the profile is for an account you already use. Say you add a profile for your work Google Account. Sign in with that account, and Chrome names the profile after it. Your work bookmarks and passwords then save to that account, and you can open them on other signed-in devices.

Stay signed out when the profile is for a shared Mac or a private task. Google's help page lists declining sign-in as the alternative. You still get a name, a photo, and a color. Nothing is saved to a Google Account while you stay signed out.

Check the account on screen before you continue. The profile name follows the account, so a wrong sign-in means a confusing name. Check the dialog first, because that takes less time than fixing a mix-up later.
Name the profile, pick a photo, and choose a color

A clear name matters more than it sounds. When several windows are open, you want to see the right profile at a glance. Work and Home are good names because they describe what the profile is for. Vague names like New Profile tell you nothing a week later.

Color helps too. Choose a color scheme that is clearly different from your other profiles. Pick a photo you recognize, so the Profile icon looks different in each window. A few seconds spent here saves you from sending a work email from a personal window.
Switch between profiles on Mac
Switching is the step you will use most. Click the Profile icon at the top right. Then choose the profile you want. Google's help page gives these exact steps.

Each profile keeps its own settings, and the Profile icon shows which one you are in. Glance at it before you type a password. That habit prevents most profile mix-ups, especially when you switch quickly between work and home.

You may see a keyboard shortcut for this. Google's Mac shortcut table lists ⇧⌘M for the profile, guest, and password menu. A third-party guide says Chrome has no native shortcut for switching profiles. The two sources conflict. Test ⇧⌘M on your own Mac, and use the Profile icon if it does not work.
Keyboard shortcuts for profiles on Mac

No official shortcut adds a profile, according to Google's Chrome shortcut table. The shortcuts below help once your profiles exist. Use them to move around quickly without hunting for the Profile icon.

items: ⇧⌘M opens the profile, guest, and password menu, according to Google's shortcut table.

blocks.text: Mistakes people make with Chrome profiles

items: Adding a profile when they meant to switch. Click the Profile icon, then choose an existing profile instead.
Signing in with a personal account on a work profile, or the reverse.
Using vague names such as Chrome or New, so profiles blur together.
Trusting a third-party menu label without checking it on screen.
Thinking Incognito is a separate profile. It runs inside the profile you are already using.

blocks.text: The sign-in mistake causes the most trouble. A profile's name follows its account. If you sign in with the wrong account, your bookmarks and passwords save to that account. Check the dialog before you click the next button, because sign-in is the step that touches your data.
Worked example: separate work and home profiles

Here is a realistic setup. You want one profile for work and one for home on the same Mac. Create the work profile first. Sign in with your work Google Account, name the profile Work, and pick a blue color scheme.

Then create the home profile from the same Profile icon menu. Stay signed out, or sign in with a personal account. Name it Home and pick a different color. Now the Profile icon looks different in each window, and your browsing stays split.
Edge cases to plan for

If the Mac is shared, a profile without sign-in keeps the account out of the way. Each person can still have a name and a color. This is simpler than sharing one profile with everyone's sign-in mixed together.

If you use Chrome on another computer too, remember that sign-in only syncs what the account saves. Google's help page says signing in saves bookmarks, passwords, and other settings, so check those on the other device. Profiles on one Mac do not change Chrome on another computer.
Troubleshooting when your screen does not match

The official help page covers the basic steps. It does not list Mac-specific error fixes, so the list below sticks to differences you can check on screen. Start with the first match, then move down the list.
What to do after you create the profile

Set up the things you want in the new profile first. Add bookmarks, check your sign-in, and set the photo. Then check the Profile icon before you browse. A profile is only as useful as the habit of checking which one is open.

Clearing history is one place where profiles matter. Clear browsing data applies to the profile you are using, so confirm the profile first. The step-by-step guide is in [clear browsing data in Chrome](/how-to/clear-browsing-data-in-chrome).
Chrome updates often. Google's homepage says there is a new Chrome update every four weeks. When a label moves, look for the same action under a new name instead of giving up.

faq.question: Can I create a Chrome profile without signing in?
faq.answer: Yes. Google's help page lists declining sign-in as the alternative to signing in. You can still name the profile, pick a photo, and choose a color scheme. Nothing is saved to a Google Account while you stay signed out.

faq.question: Is a Chrome profile the same as a Mac user account?
faq.answer: No. A Chrome profile lives inside Chrome and controls browser data and settings. A Mac user account is a separate login for the whole computer. Use profiles to split your browsing, and use user accounts to split the computer.

faq.question: How do I switch to another profile on Mac?
faq.answer: Click the Profile icon at the top right of the Chrome window, then choose the profile you want. Google's help page gives these exact steps. Some guides also mention ⇧⌘M for the profile menu.

faq.question: Does ⇧⌘M create a new profile?
faq.answer: No. Google's Mac shortcut table lists ⇧⌘M for the profile, guest, and password menu. It is not an add-profile shortcut. No official shortcut adds a profile, according to that table.

faq.question: Why do the menu labels in my Chrome look different?
faq.answer: Chrome changes often. Google says there is a new update every four weeks, and labels can move between releases. Follow what your screen shows, and treat older guides with care.

faq.question: Is there a Chrome web app for profiles?
faq.answer: No separate web app for profiles came up in our check. Profile creation happens in the desktop Chrome browser on your Mac.

task: Create a Chrome profile on Mac
appliesTo: Google Chrome desktop on macOS, Profile icon and menu bar routes
requirements: A Mac with Google Chrome installed
A Google Account, only if you want to sign in (optional)
A few free minutes and an open Chrome window

steps.name: Open Google Chrome
steps.text: Open Chrome from the Dock, Launchpad, or your Applications folder. Any open Chrome window works, so you do not need to close your tabs first.
steps.tip: If Chrome is already open, skip this step and go to the next one.

steps.name: Click the Profile icon
steps.text: Look at the top right of the Chrome window. Click the Profile icon. It shows the picture of the profile you are using right now.
steps.tip: If you cannot find it, check that the front window is Chrome and not another browser.

steps.name: Choose Add Chrome profile
steps.text: In the menu that opens, click Add Chrome profile. That is the label Google's help page uses. Menus can change between releases, so match the wording on your screen.

steps.name: Sign in or stay signed out
steps.text: To sign in, enter the Google Account you want to use. Chrome then names the profile after that Account. To skip sign-in, decline it and continue. Google's help page lists declining as the alternative.
steps.tip: Check which account the dialog shows before you continue.

steps.name: Pick a name, photo, and color
steps.text: Type a name that tells you what the profile is for, such as Work or Home. Choose a photo and a color scheme. Then finish the setup.
steps.tip: Pick a color you will not confuse with your other profiles.

steps.name: Menu bar route, if your screen shows it
steps.text: Click Profiles in the menu bar, then choose Add Profile. This label comes from a third-party guide, not from Google's help page. If your menu bar has no Profiles menu, use the Profile icon route.

steps.name: The ⋮ button route, if you use it
steps.text: Click the ⋮ button at the top right of Chrome. Choose your current profile name. Then click Add New Profile, and continue with the naming and sign-in choices above.

shortcuts.action: Open the profile, guest, and password menu

troubleshooting.problem: The Profile icon is not in the top right
troubleshooting.fix: Check that the front window is Google Chrome, not another browser. Google's help page places the icon at the top right. If it still does not show, use the ⋮ button route in the steps above.

troubleshooting.problem: Your menu says different words than this guide
troubleshooting.fix: Chrome labels can change between releases. Google's homepage says a new update arrives every four weeks. Follow the wording on your screen and look for the same action.

troubleshooting.problem: The sign-in dialog has no Stay signed out button
troubleshooting.fix: Google's help page describes declining sign-in as the alternative. Look for a decline or skip option in the dialog. The Stay signed out label comes from a third-party guide, so the wording may differ.

troubleshooting.problem: ⇧⌘M does nothing, or guides disagree about it
troubleshooting.fix: Google's shortcut table lists ⇧⌘M for the profile, guest, and password menu. ShiftPlus says Chrome has no native switch shortcut. Test it on your Mac, and use the Profile icon if the shortcut fails.

troubleshooting.problem: You cannot tell which guide to trust
troubleshooting.fix: Use Google's help page for the core steps. Use third-party guides for extra detail, and check their publication dates. Google's page covers all desktop platforms, not only Mac.
